content: Glossophobia, also known as speech anxiety, refers to the fear of public speaking. The term originates from the Greek words glōssa, meaning tongue, and phobos, meaning fear or dread. Glossophobia is often considered a symptom of stage fright. Symptoms Individuals with glossophobia may experience intense anxiety even at the thought of having to verbally communicate with a group. They may avoid events where they would be the focus of attention, and they might experience physical distress, nausea, or feelings of panic in such situations. The symptoms of speech anxiety can be categorized into three groups: physical, verbal, and non-verbal. Physical symptoms are caused by the autonomic nervous system's fight or flight response to the situation. These include acute hearing, increased heart rate, elevated blood pressure, dilated pupils, excessive perspiration, increased oxygen intake, stiffening of neck and upper back muscles, and dry mouth. Verbal symptoms may include a tense or quivering voice, as well as frequent use of filler words like um and ah, which are often used as a coping mechanism by anxious speakers. In some cases, individuals may experience dysfunctional speech anxiety, where the intensity of the fight or flight response prevents them from performing effectively. Many people report stress-induced speech disorders that only occur during public speaking. Interestingly, some individuals with glossophobia can perform in public, such as dancing or acting, as long as they do not have to speak. Others may be able to speak or sing in public if they cannot see the audience or if they adopt a character or stage persona, distancing themselves from their personal identity. Causes The underlying causes of glossophobia are often self-defeating thoughts and anxiety-provoking situations. Self-defeating thoughts include imagining oneself failing, believing that everything must be perfect, and seeking complete approval from others. Anxiety-provoking situations are those that hold significant importance to the speaker, situations where the speaker is the center of attention, or scenarios where the speaker feels subordinate to the audience. Help and Relief Organizations such as Toastmasters International and International Training in Communication, as well as public speaking training courses, can help individuals manage their fear to more tolerable levels. Self-help materials on public speaking are among the most popular topics in the self-help genre. Additionally, some individuals turn to medications, such as beta-blockers, to temporarily alleviate their symptoms of glossophobia.
